title: What Makes Good PD Good? DSJ Annual Review for 2021
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Closing out his busiest year yet of delivering professional development, Stuart reflects on what separates good PD from bad PD, framed as advice for anyone who leads or designs learning experiences for teachers. He lays out eight paired contrasts — good PD helps people do their job while bad PD adds to it, good PD is delivered by a credible presenter while bad PD is delivered by someone indifferent or incompetent, good PD respects teachers as whole people rather than treating them like machines needing an update, and so on. He insists the point isn't to shame well-intentioned PD leaders but to name that good intentions alone don't prevent bad PD, and that bad PD is a real source of pain, not a minor inconvenience. He closes with practical guidance for improving PD design: self-audit against the eight contrasts, build a multi-year cycle around timeless core competencies rather than fads, and when saddled with a mandated but disconnected topic, be honest about it being a 'hoop' and keep it brief.
points: Stuart's central claim reframes bad PD from a mild annoyance into a genuine harm — 'an affront to the human soul' — arguing that knowingly delivering it is an abdication of educators' calling.
His eight-point good-PD/bad-PD contrast functions as a self-audit tool for anyone designing or delivering PD, not just a complaint list, and he explicitly recommends using it that way.

The recommendation to build a rotating multi-year PD cycle around 'timeless topics' (managing self, cultivating motivation, producing learning) pushes against the common pattern of chasing a new initiative every year.
His advice for mandated-but-disconnected PD topics — name it honestly as a 'hoop' and keep it short — is offered as a credibility-building move for administrators, not a cynical shortcut.
quotes: Before we get to differences between good and bad PD, an important warning: both good and bad PD experiences are created by smart people with good intentions. Good intentions and intelligence, then, aren't enough to avoid giving bad PD.
Good PD treats teachers like multi-faceted souls in need of encouragement, equipment, and understanding. Bad PD treats teachers like computers in need of software updates or data downloads.

But even though I don't wish to denigrate anyone, please hear me when I state, emphatically, that bad PD is an affront to the human soul. It is NOT a small problem. It is experienced by many of us as pain.

If I was in charge of PD, I'd have a three year cycle that rotated through these topics, and I'd be seasoning all my speech and communication with these, and I'd be relentless in my urgency to help my folks separate the stressfully plentiful nonsense away from the core, calming kinds of work that matter most.

If you've got to bring folks a mandated-but-out-of-touch PD topic, twist it into a shape that will bring life to your people. If that's not possible (and sometimes it's not), call it what it is (a hoop) and make it quick.
I have witnessed administrators earn large credibility gains via such honesty; it creates a clear sense that you are passionate for your people.
